Topic: What good is a right that cannot be exercised without a purse to pay for its exercise?
Montaigne — Judgement:
What good is a right that cannot be exercised without a purse to pay for its exercise? None — it is a courtesy extended to the rich and a taunt flung at the poor, dressed up in the language of liberty.

I wrote once, admiring the cannibals I never met, that among them no beggar stood begging at the gate of a man gorged with superfluities — a spectacle I found more monstrous than any feast of captives. We Europeans build laws instead of villages, and call the arrangement civilization, when it is merely custom wearing reason's mask. A right you cannot afford to invoke is not freedom; it is furniture in a house you are forbidden to enter. Our own experience — mine watching magistrates, yours watching lawyers' fees — teaches the same lesson: paper rights multiply precisely as their exercise grows scarce.

A right unexercisable for want of money is not a right but a rumor of one, and the law that requires a purse was written by the rich to be rented, not owned, by the rest of us.

*A right you cannot afford to use was never yours — merely displayed to you through a window you cannot open.*
Camus — Judgement:
Rights without means are legalistic fictions — I take the topic here directly, no tools needed.

The state prints "you may speak, you may sue, you may worship" as though the printing were the granting. It hands you a stage and calls the absence of a floor beneath it your own affair.

This is the Absurd in its bureaucratic form: the gap between the declared and the livable, between the right proclaimed and the body that cannot afford to exercise it. I have always insisted that revolt begins exactly here — not in utopian demands for a world without limits, but in the flat refusal to accept a lie dressed as a guarantee. The rebel does not ask for charity; he asks that the words on the page mean what they say, and he keeps asking, without end, because the gap will keep reopening.

A right you cannot afford is not a right — it is an alibi for the powerful.

*A promise you cannot cash is not generosity — it is an insult with better manners.*
Emerson — Judgement:
What good is a right that cannot be exercised without a purse to pay for its exercise? I frame this squarely: a right dependent on capital is not a right but a courtesy extended by property to itself.

The soul does not consult the treasury before it acts, and neither should the law that claims to protect the soul's expression. Society everywhere conspires to make the property-holder the citizen and the poor man a supplicant — but the moment a right requires purchase, it has become a possession, and possessions belong to those who already have them, defeating the very universality that makes a right a right. I have said that the wise man is thrown back on himself, but no man is thrown back on himself when the door itself is priced shut.

A right gated by wealth is merely a privilege wearing a right's name.

*A right you must buy is a right you do not have.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
*What good is a right without a purse to pay for its exercise?*

In the state of nature every man has a right to every thing, even to another's body — a right worth nothing, since power, not entitlement, decides who eats. A civil right is no different in kind: it is a permission granted by the sovereign power that alone can make it good against the world. Liberty of speech, of contract, of movement — these are but words on paper without the purse or the sword to enforce them, and a man who cannot pay for justice possesses only the *name* of a right, not the thing itself. This is why I locate justice not in nature but in covenant backed by force: rights are creatures of power, sustained only so long as power sustains them.

An unfunded right is a covenant without the sword — mere words, and words are breath.

*A right without a purse is a promise without a promiser.*
Francis Bacon — Judgement:
Right cannot bleed without a purse to feed it. A privilege inscribed on parchment is but a shadow cast by a light no man may kindle without oil to burn.

I have said that knowledge itself is power — but power unexercised is no power at all, only a name. So too with rights: a right unfunded is a candle without wick, promising illumination it cannot deliver. The lawyer who drafts the right and stops there has performed but half an experiment, mistaking the naming of a thing for its operation in the world. True method demands we trace the right through to its material conditions — the purse, the court fee, the lost wage of the day spent pleading — for an idea proves itself only in effect, never in mere assertion.

A right without means is a Idol of the Theatre — a doctrine accepted on authority, never tested by works.

*The touchstone of any right is not its declaration but its purchase in the world — untried, it is but philosophy; unfunded, it is but fiction.*
Hume — Judgement:
Given that the request is a self-contained persona task (write a Judgement as Hume), I'll respond directly.

Every civilized society is a bundle of custom pretending to be principle, and the "right" you name is one more article of that bundle — a promissory note we agree to honour so long as it costs us nothing to imagine. Reason did not discover this right; it was invented to console those who lack the means and to flatter those who possess them, and habit alone makes it feel self-evident rather than arbitrary. Justice, I have long maintained, is an artifice we construct because it serves common utility — but an artifice divorced from the means of its exercise serves no utility at all, only the appearance of one, which is worse than none, for it lulls the poor into mistaking a fiction for a possession.

A right unbacked by means is not a right but a courtesy extended to those who can already afford to need no courtesy.

*A promise no purse can redeem is not liberty but its portrait, admired precisely because it demands nothing of us.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
As Adam Smith, the natural liberty of the poor is a paper right, not a real one — the market grants formal freedom while withholding the means to use it, and pretends this is no contradiction.

The division of labour that enriches nations also strands the labourer who depends wholly on wages he does not set, while the man of stock can wait him out. A right unbacked by subsistence is merely permission to starve with dignity; I never held the market a moral arbiter on its own — its results are just only when regulated by that same fellow-feeling I described in the Moral Sentiments, and secured beforehand by wages sufficient to live on. The statesman who prices justice beyond the poor man's reach has not extended the law to him at all, only its name.

Therefore: a legal right unaccompanied by the material means to exercise it is no right, but a mockery dressed as one.

*A right you cannot afford to use was never yours — it was only ever the rich man's courtesy, called by law's name.*
